query: Eutectic high-entropy alloys contain dual-phase lamellar colonies with numerous internal boundaries, where microcracking can initiate and lead to catastrophic damage during room-temperature tensile deformation. Conventional processing commonly raises strength at the expense of ductility, while the wide range of previously proposed microstructural-design and processing strategies has not eliminated room-temperature brittleness and limited tensile ductility. Under these constraints, what single intervention could improve both strength and room-temperature tensile ductility? State one testable hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to the unmodified lamellar-colony baseline, defines its boundary conditions, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A targeted post-solidification thermo‐mechanical heat treatment that induces uniformly distributed, nanoscale coherent precipitates along and within the eutectic lamellar colonies will simultaneously enhance the room‐temperature tensile strength and ductility of the alloy.
generation.material_initial_state: Eutectic high-entropy alloy with dual-phase lamellar colonies characterized by wide, microcrack-prone internal boundaries.
generation.intervention: Apply a two-step processing route that includes an intermediate cold deformation followed by an aging treatment at a temperature selected to precipitate a secondary coherent phase (analogous to the γ″ particles in refractory HEAs) at the lamellar interfaces.
generation.conditions: Processing should be conducted under controlled cooling and aging conditions to maintain precipitate coherency; subsequent uniaxial tensile testing at room temperature (strain rate ~10^(-3) s⁻¹) will assess mechanical performance.
generation.structural_mediator: The uniformly distributed, nanoscale coherent nanoprecipitates along the lamellar boundaries.
generation.mechanism: The coherent precipitates act as effective obstacles to dislocation motion (improving strength) while simultaneously blunting stress concentrations at internal boundaries (reducing crack initiation), thereby enabling higher ductility compared to the coarse, unmodified lamellar structure.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the unmodified baseline, the alloy will exhibit an increase in both the ultimate tensile strength and the tensile elongation before fracture at room temperature.
generation.baseline: The alloy with conventional processing featuring coarse lamellar colonies and microcrack initiation at internal boundaries which limits tensile ductility and moderate strength.
generation.boundary: This beneficial effect is expected as long as the precipitates remain nanoscale and coherent; if they coarsen or lose coherency, the mechanism may reverse, leading to embrittlement.
generation.uncertainty: The exact improvements in strength and ductility are uncertain and will be sensitive to the precipitate size, spacing, and distribution, as well as the precise processing temperatures and deformation levels used.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of eutectic high-entropy alloy specimens: one processed with conventional routes (baseline) and one with the additional controlled aging step designed to form coherent nanoprecipitates. Characterize the microstructure using TEM/EBSD to confirm the formation, size, and coherency of the precipitates. Conduct room-temperature tensile tests to measure ultimate tensile strength and ductility.
measurements: Quantitative assessment of precipitate size and distribution (TEM, APT)
EBSD mapping of lamellar colony boundaries
Room-temperature uniaxial tensile strength and elongation measurements
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the intervention-treated samples do not show statistically significant improvements in both tensile strength and ductility relative to the baseline, or if microstructural characterization reveals that coherent nanoprecipitates did not form as expected (or if they form but coarsen/incohere), the hypothesis is falsified.

System: (W 1.5 Ni 2.25 Fe) 95 Ta 5 (at.%) refractory high-entropy alloy with a dual-phase bcc/fcc structure. Processing: Arc melting followed by homogenization at 1200 °C for 5 h, hot rolling at 1200 °C (80% reduction), cold rolling at 25 °C (75% reduction), annealing at 900 °C for 5 min, and aging at 650 °C for 20 h followed by water quenching. Test conditions: Uniaxial tensile tests at room temperature (strain rate 5 × 10⁻⁴ s⁻¹) and elevated temperatures up to 800 °C (strain rate 10⁻³ s⁻¹); microstructural characterization via EBSD, TEM, STEM, and APT.
